cards.ifItFails: He blames you convincingly enough that you start believing the criticism is fair and try harder to fix yourself. Stop there — a sudden switch in tone is data about him, not a grade on you. Say to a friend, not him: "This started right when he mentioned someone new — that's not a coincidence."
cards.counter:
If someone's warmth toward you drops sharply with no clear cause, check the timeline against a new name.
• Notice sudden criticism replacing old warmth.
• Ask what changed, plainly, once.
• Stop trying to earn back affection that disappeared for reasons that aren't about you. Don't confront him about a new name before you have more than one clue — a wrong accusation hands him the upper hand in the fight.
cards.insight: Devaluation is cheaper for him than an honest breakup — it makes you push him away instead. The harder part is not turning the criticism inward before you've checked if it's even true.
cards.example: For two weeks, Hannah's boyfriend suddenly criticized things about her that never bothered him before. She noticed a new coworker's name had started coming up in his stories around the same time. She stopped apologizing her way back to his old warmth and asked him directly what changed — his answer confirmed what she already suspected.

cards.title: Blame Timing So He's Never The Bad Guy
cards.remember: It's never him leaving you. It's always 'the timing.'
cards.hook: 'I'm just not ready.' 'My job is crazy right now.' Never 'I don't want this' — always something outside him.
cards.truth:
Blaming circumstances lets him leave without owning the choice.
• He names a reason outside himself — work, timing, 'not being ready.'
• You're left arguing with a circumstance instead of a decision, which nobody wins.
• Most people try to fix the circumstance. The circumstance was never the real reason.
cards.when: He gives you an external reason for pulling back — timing, work, distance — instead of a direct answer.
cards.theySee: A woman trying to solve a problem — offering to wait, to adjust plans, to make the timing work.

signals.t: He blames 'timing' or 'where I'm at' without naming what would fix it.
The reason sounds solvable, which keeps you trying to solve it.
He never proposes an alternative plan or a real date to revisit it.
The same 'timing' reason gets repeated months later, unchanged.

steps.title: Ask what would fix it
steps.desc: Ask directly: 'What would need to change for the timing to work?'

steps.title: Listen for specifics
steps.desc: Check if his answer names an actual condition or stays vague.

steps.title: Stop offering fixes
steps.desc: Don't propose solutions to a problem he hasn't defined clearly.

cards.script: "What specifically would need to change? Not 'the timing' — what, exactly?"
cards.watchFor: He can't name a specific condition, or the condition keeps moving when you meet it.
cards.ifItFails: He names something specific, you meet it, and the goalpost moves again to a new vague reason. That's confirmation the reason was never the reason. Say: "I met the thing you named and it changed nothing, so I'm done adjusting for this."
cards.counter:
If someone blames an external circumstance for pulling back, test whether the circumstance is real.
• Ask what specifically would need to change.
• Notice if the answer stays vague or keeps moving.
• Stop offering to fix a problem that was never named clearly. Don't keep negotiating past the second broken deadline — that's no longer information-gathering, that's you doing his work for him.
cards.insight: Blaming timing keeps him likable and keeps you working the problem. The real tell isn't the excuse — it's whether he ever proposes a plan to revisit it.
cards.example: Ben told Sofia the timing 'just wasn't right' for him to commit. She asked what specifically would need to change. He named his work travel schedule — she waited for it to calm down, and when it did, the excuse just moved to something else. She stopped adjusting for him after that.

cards.title: Get So Bad You Have To Be The One Who Leaves
cards.principle: Passive Withdrawal As A Forced-Abandonment Strategy
cards.remember: He gets worse on purpose so you do the breaking up.
cards.hook: He stops trying. He picks fights over nothing. He's not falling apart — he's making you throw the punch.
cards.truth:
Being the one who gets left is cheaper than being the one who leaves.
• He withdraws effort, picks small fights, and stops showing up the way he used to.
• You end up ending it, so he never has to say 'I don't want this.'
• Most people blame themselves for 'giving up.' He built the exit for you to walk through.
cards.when: He's become distant and difficult without ever saying he wants out, and you're the one thinking about ending it.
cards.theySee: A partner who seems checked out, unbothered, or is picking unnecessary fights.

signals.t: He stops initiating plans, calls, or affection without any stated reason.
Small arguments start over things that never bothered him before.
He seems calm or relieved during arguments instead of upset.
He never directly says he wants to end things, no matter how bad it gets.

steps.title: Name the pattern out loud
steps.desc: Say plainly: 'It feels like you're trying to get me to end this.'

steps.title: Ask him to say it
steps.desc: Ask directly: 'Do you want to end this? Just say it.'

steps.title: Don't do the work for him
steps.desc: If he won't answer, stop absorbing the blame for ending it.

cards.script: "If you want this to end, say that. Don't make me do it so you don't have to."
cards.watchFor: He deflects the direct question instead of giving a real yes or no.
cards.ifItFails: He denies wanting to end it but nothing changes in his behavior afterward. Treat the denial as noise and the behavior as the answer. Say: "Your actions already answered this, I'm not waiting for the words anymore," and act on that.
cards.counter:
If someone withdraws and starts fights without ever naming what they want, that ambiguity is doing work for them.
• Notice effort dropping with no stated reason.
• Ask directly if they want to end it.
• Refuse to carry the guilt of ending something they engineered. Don't stay to win the standoff of who leaves first — the cost of staying outweighs the point you'd prove.
cards.insight: Making you the one who leaves protects his story, not your feelings. The harder move is ending it cleanly anyway, even knowing he'll tell people you're the one who walked.
cards.example: Derek stopped initiating plans and started picking fights over nothing, but never once said he wanted out. Priya finally said, 'If you want this to end, say that — don't make me do it.' He denied it but nothing changed, so she ended it herself two weeks later, done waiting for the words.

cards.title: Write Down His Story So You Can Catch It Change
cards.remember: Write down what he says. Check it again in a month.
cards.hook: He told you he doesn't talk to his ex. Three weeks later, the story has quietly changed.
cards.truth:
A true story stays the same over time. A built one drifts.
• You remember the gist of what someone says, not the exact words.
• A practiced talker counts on that fuzziness to update details later.
• Most people trust memory over notes. Notes don't forget.
cards.when: You want to check if what he's telling you stays consistent over weeks.
cards.theySee: A woman who listens closely, asks good follow-up questions, remembers details.

signals.t: A specific detail — a date, a name, a reason — changes slightly when he retells it.
He looks briefly thrown when you reference something he said before.
The updated version conveniently fixes a problem with the old one.
He recovers fast and smooths over the inconsistency without addressing it.

steps.title: Keep a private note
steps.desc: After key conversations, write down names, dates, and claims he made.

steps.title: Bring it up later, casually
steps.desc: Reference an old detail naturally in a later conversation.

steps.title: Watch the gap
steps.desc: Compare his new version to your note, without announcing you're checking.

cards.script: "Wait, didn't you say her name was Jess, not Jen?"
cards.watchFor: He corrects the story too smoothly, without pausing to actually remember.
cards.ifItFails: He has a plausible explanation for the change and it might even be true — people misremember things too. Don't build a case on one inconsistency. Keep the note going and wait for a second one before deciding it's a pattern.
cards.counter:
This defense can be turned on you too — don't let someone run a memory test on you unnoticed.
• Notice if you're being asked to recall exact past statements under pressure.
• Say: "I don't remember exactly, let me think about it," instead of guessing.
• Keep your own notes so you're not relying only on memory either.
cards.insight: One drifted detail could be nothing. The harder part is trusting your own notes over the warm feeling that he'd never lie to you.
cards.example: Early on, Kayla noted that her date said his ex's name was Jess. Three weeks later he called her Jen. Kayla mentioned it casually, and he corrected it a little too smoothly — she kept the note running instead of letting it go.

cards.title: Turn His Someday Into A Date On The Calendar
cards.remember: A promise with no date isn't a promise. Ask for the date.
cards.hook: 'Someday we'll travel together' sounds nice. It also can't ever be wrong, because it can't ever be checked.
cards.truth:
A vague promise can never fail, so it can be repeated forever for free.
• Every 'someday' claim can be converted into a specific, checkable date.
• A person who means it will name one. A person who doesn't will dodge.
• Most people accept the vague version because asking for a date feels pushy.
cards.when: He makes a future promise with no specific date, and you're deciding whether to take it seriously.
cards.theySee: A partner asking a reasonable, grounded question instead of just accepting a nice-sounding promise.

signals.t: He says 'someday' or 'eventually' instead of naming a month.
He resists when you ask for an actual date, calling it 'too much pressure.'
The same vague promise resurfaces months later, unchanged.
He'll give you a date for small things but never for the big promise.

steps.title: Ask for the month
steps.desc: When he makes a future promise, ask what month it would happen.

steps.title: Write it down
steps.desc: Note the answer, even a vague one, so you can check it later.

steps.title: Revisit at the deadline
steps.desc: When the date arrives, bring it up directly, whether or not it happened.

cards.script: "Okay — someday like this year, or someday like 'never actually'?"
cards.watchFor: He laughs it off instead of naming an actual timeframe.
cards.ifItFails: He gives a date just to end the conversation, then quietly misses it without comment. Don't let the missed date pass in silence — that silence is the actual answer. Say: "That date came and went. What's the new one, or is there one?"
cards.counter:
Know when not to run this move too: don't turn every casual comment into a contract demand.
• Notice if you're demanding dates for things that were never meant as promises.
• Reserve this for repeated, specific promises, not throwaway comments.
• Save it for patterns, not single sentences.
cards.insight: A promise with a date attached can be broken, which is exactly why some people never attach one. The harder part is asking for the date without apologizing for wanting it.
cards.example: Every few months, Alex's boyfriend brought up 'someday' traveling together, with no month ever attached. She finally asked, 'someday like this year, or someday like never?' He laughed it off instead of naming a date, and she stopped counting the promise as real after that.

cards.title: Keep Your Own Friends In The Loop The Whole Time
cards.principle: Maintain External Support Network — Isolation Countermeasure
cards.remember: Tell your friends everything as it happens, not after it's bad.
cards.hook: You don't need a red flag to call your friend. Tell her the small stuff too, before you need her to believe you.
cards.truth:
An outside view only works if it has information to work with.
• Isolation usually happens slowly, one skipped hangout at a time.
• A friend who's heard the small updates can spot the pattern faster than you can.
• Most people only call a friend once something feels wrong. By then, the friend is behind.
cards.when: You're a few weeks or months into something new and haven't been telling friends the details as they happen.
cards.theySee: A friend who's a little quieter lately, who used to text every detail and now shares less.

signals.t: You've told your friends less about him this month than last month.
You've canceled plans with friends more often since seeing him.
You catch yourself leaving details out when you do talk to friends about him.
A friend has already asked if everything's okay, unprompted.

steps.title: Send the small updates
steps.desc: Text a friend the boring details too, not just the big moments.

steps.title: Keep the standing plans
steps.desc: Don't cancel recurring friend time for him more than once in a row.

steps.title: Ask for the blunt read
steps.desc: Ask a friend directly: 'Has anything I've told you sounded off to you?'

cards.script: "Random update: he did this thing today, no big deal, just keeping you posted."
cards.watchFor: Your friend's reaction to a 'no big deal' update tells you if it actually is one.
cards.ifItFails: You keep sending updates but notice you're still quietly editing out the parts that don't look great. That's worth noticing on its own. Say to the friend directly: "I think I've been leaving stuff out — can I just tell you the whole thing?"
cards.counter:
This is already the defense move — the failure mode is doing it performatively instead of honestly.
• Notice if your updates to friends are all positive, with nothing uncertain.
• Include the confusing or uncomfortable moments, not just the good ones.
• Let a friend push back without getting defensive about it.
cards.insight: A friend who's heard everything can catch a pattern you're too close to see. The harder part is sending the boring update on a day when nothing feels wrong yet.
cards.example: Three months into dating someone new, Talia realized she'd stopped sending her friend the small daily updates she used to share. She started again, on purpose, texting even boring details. Her friend caught something in a 'no big deal' story that Talia hadn't noticed herself.
